blocks.text: A 62-year-old farmer has a nosebleed at dinner. He tips his head back, swallows a mouthful of blood and vomits it across the table. Within minutes the bleeding is heavier, not lighter. The first-aid mistakes people make are as instructive as the correct manoeuvre.

blocks.markdown: **Anatomy of a nosebleed.** The nasal septum is supplied by branches of both the internal carotid (anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries) and the external carotid (sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries). On the anterior septum these meet in **Little's area** (Kiesselbach's plexus), a thin, exposed mucosa where most bleeds arise (*anterior epistaxis*). Less commonly, bleeding comes from the posterior nasal cavity, usually the sphenopalatine territory (*posterior epistaxis*), in older or hypertensive patients, and is heavy, bilateral or runs into the throat.

blocks.title: First aid
blocks.text: Sit up, **lean forward** (so blood is not swallowed or aspirated), pinch the **soft, fleshy part** of the nose (below the bony bridge) with thumb and finger, and maintain firm pressure **continuously for 10 to 15 minutes** without peeking. Spit out blood, breathe through the mouth, and apply a cold compress if desired. Do not tilt the head back or lie flat, and do not pinch the bony bridge.

blocks.markdown: **Causes and assessment.** Digital trauma, dry air, upper respiratory infection and nasal sprays are common local causes; hypertension, anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs, alcohol, haematological disorders and hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia are systemic contributors. In an adult, *unilateral persistent* bleeding with obstruction suggests a tumour, and in an adolescent boy a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Assess **airway, breathing and circulation first**, estimate blood loss, place IV access and send FBC, coagulation screen and group and save in significant bleeds, then examine the nose with a headlight and nasal speculum after clots are cleared.

rows: 1. First aid
Always first
Lean forward, pinch soft nose 10-15 min
Most stop
2. Cautery
Visible anterior bleeding point, bleeding stopped or controlled
Silver nitrate or electrical cautery after topical anaesthetic
Cauterise one side only (septal perforation risk)
3. Anterior packing
Cautery fails or no point seen
Nasal tampon or inflatable pack, or ribbon gauze
Review in 24 to 48 hours; antibiotics per local policy (check BNF)
4. Posterior control
Bleeding persists behind the pack or blood in the throat
Posterior balloon or tampon; admit
Monitor; sedation and oxygen saturation observed
5. Surgical or radiological
Failed packing
Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation
ENT and interventional radiology

blocks.title: Worked example: a patient losing blood
blocks.prompt: A 71-year-old man on aspirin and treated hypertension has had heavy bleeding for 40 minutes despite pressure. He is pale. Heart rate 112/min and systolic BP 100 mmHg. Blood runs down the back of his throat. Outline management.

steps.text: Airway and circulation: sit him up, give oxygen, establish IV access and take bloods (FBC, clotting, group and save). The shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) is 112/100 = 1.12, higher than the normal of about 0.5 to 0.7, suggesting significant volume loss.
Blood in the oropharynx despite pressure suggests a posterior bleed or an ineffective anterior seal.
Try to identify the site and place an anterior pack bilaterally or a posterior balloon, with senior ENT input; admit for observation and correct fluids or coagulopathy (review antiplatelets).
If packing fails, escalate to endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation.

blocks.answer: Significant bleed with probable posterior component: resuscitate, pack, admit and escalate to ENT.

blocks.caption: A bedside estimate of haemodynamic compromise; values above about 0.9 to 1 suggest shock, but cut-offs vary and beta-blockers or older age alter its reliability.

blocks.markdown: **Tonsillitis and its complications.** Acute tonsillitis is common and usually self-limiting. When infection breaks through the tonsillar capsule into the potential space between the capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor, a **peritonsillar abscess** (quinsy) forms. Typical features: a few days of sore throat, then severe *unilateral* throat pain, **trismus** (difficulty opening the mouth), a muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling, fever, and on examination a swollen soft palate with the **uvula pushed to the opposite side**. Treatment is needle aspiration or incision and drainage, IV or appropriate antibiotics, analgesia and fluids per local guidance (check BNF); recurrent episodes may lead to tonsillectomy.

blocks.title: Deep neck space infection
blocks.text: Infection may spread along fascial planes: the *parapharyngeal* space, the *retropharyngeal* space (especially in young children after pharyngitis or from penetrating injury) and the floor of the mouth (*Ludwig's angina*, bilateral submandibular infection usually from a lower molar). Suspect it in a patient with fever, neck swelling or stiffness (torticollis), trismus, dysphagia, drooling, muffled voice or stridor. The **airway can close suddenly**, and infection can reach the mediastinum or carotid sheath. Priorities: secure the airway with senior anaesthetic and ENT help (do not lie the patient flat), IV antibiotics, contrast CT, and surgical drainage when collections are seen.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting a sore throat
blocks.prompt: A 19-year-old has had a sore throat for 4 days, now with severe left-sided pain, a temperature of 38.5 C, difficulty opening the mouth and a muffled voice. The left tonsil is displaced medially with swelling of the soft palate; the uvula points to the right. He can swallow saliva but is drooling. Interpret.

steps.text: Unilateral pain, trismus, muffled voice and a displaced tonsil with uvular deviation away from the lesion point to peritonsillar abscess rather than simple tonsillitis.
Stridor and a hot swollen neck are not described, but the drooling and trismus need monitoring of the airway; examine for neck swelling and signs of deeper spread.
Management: refer for same-day ENT assessment; aspiration or incision and drainage under local anaesthetic, IV antibiotics and fluids per protocol (check BNF), analgesia.
If there were neck swelling, stridor or systemic toxicity, a contrast CT would look for a parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal collection.

blocks.answer: Peritonsillar abscess: drainage, antibiotics and airway vigilance.

blocks.markdown: **Assessing a neck lump.** The aim is to decide quickly whether a lump is reactive, congenital, inflammatory or malignant. *History*: age; duration; pain; fever; sore throat or tooth problems; hoarseness, dysphagia, stridor; unilateral ear pain with a normal ear; smoking, alcohol or betel nut use; HPV or EBV risk; night sweats and weight loss; previous cancer. *Examination*: describe site (by anatomical level or triangle), size, consistency, mobility, tenderness, skin changes, and whether it moves on swallowing (thyroid) or on tongue protrusion (thyroglossal cyst, midline). Examine the thyroid, salivary glands, scalp and skin, and the **upper aerodigestive tract** (oral cavity, oropharynx, nasal cavity, nasopharynx and larynx, by nasendoscopy). *Investigations*: ultrasound with fine needle aspiration cytology or core biopsy; CT or MRI and PET-CT for staging; panendoscopy. **Avoid open excisional biopsy of a suspected malignant node as a first step** because of the risk of tumour seeding.

rows: Hard, fixed, painless neck lump over 3 weeks, especially a unilateral level II to IV node in an adult smoker
Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma
Persistent hoarseness over 3 weeks, especially in smokers
Laryngeal cancer
Unilateral otalgia with a normal ear
Referred pain from oropharynx or larynx
Persistent unilateral sore throat or non-healing oral ulcer over 3 weeks
Oropharyngeal or oral cancer
Unilateral nasal obstruction or bleeding, serous otitis in an adult
Nasal or nasopharyngeal tumour
Dysphagia, weight loss, stridor
Advanced pharyngeal, laryngeal or oesophageal disease
blocks.caption: Red flags for head and neck cancer (use current NICE NG12 criteria for referral thresholds)

points: Epistaxis first aid is sit forward and pinch the soft nose for 10 to 15 minutes; escalate through cautery, anterior pack, posterior control and surgery or embolisation while resuscitating if bleeding is heavy.
Peritonsillar abscess gives unilateral severe pain, trismus, a muffled voice and uvular deviation; deep neck space infections threaten the airway and need urgent senior and imaging input.

A persistent neck lump over three weeks in an adult needs examination of the upper aerodigestive tract, ultrasound with sampling, and urgent referral if red flags are present; avoid open biopsy as a first step.
Antibiotics, topical agents and referral thresholds must be checked against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has a spontaneous nosebleed at school after picking his nose. Which advice is correct?

options.text: Sit upright leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes
Lie flat with the head tilted back and pinch the bony bridge
Pack the nostril tightly with cotton wool
Blow the nose repeatedly to clear the clot

questions.correctOptionText: Sit upright leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes

distractorRationale.b: Leads to swallowing or aspirating blood; pressure is not on the bleeding area.
distractorRationale.c: May traumatise the mucosa and does not give effective pressure.
distractorRationale.d: Dislodges the clot and prolongs bleeding.

questions.explanation: Leaning forward prevents swallowing and aspiration of blood, and pinching the soft part of the nose compresses Little's area on the anterior septum. Pressure must be continuous for 10 to 15 minutes. Tilting the head back or pinching the bridge is ineffective.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old hypertensive woman on aspirin has a heavy nosebleed lasting an hour despite bilateral anterior nasal packs. Blood is running down the back of her throat and she is pale. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Resuscitate with IV access and bloods, admit, and arrange posterior packing or balloon with ENT support
Remove packs and send her home with antibiotics
Silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the septum
Wait for the bleeding to stop spontaneously

questions.correctOptionText: Resuscitate with IV access and bloods, admit, and arrange posterior packing or balloon with ENT support

distractorRationale.a: Correct: probable posterior bleed with haemodynamic effects.
distractorRationale.c: Bilateral cautery risks septal perforation, and the site is posterior.
distractorRationale.d: Not safe in a heavy bleed.

questions.explanation: Failed anterior packing with blood in the oropharynx indicates a posterior source. She needs resuscitation, admission, posterior control with ENT and consideration of surgical ligation or embolisation if packing fails.

questions.stem: A man with epistaxis has a heart rate of 124 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure of 96 mmHg. Calculate his shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Shock index = 124 / 96 = 1.29. Values above about 0.9 to 1 suggest significant hypovolaemia, though thresholds vary and the index is unreliable in patients taking rate-limiting drugs.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl had a sore throat last week and now has a fever, refuses to swallow, drools, and holds her neck stiffly tilted to one side. She is sitting still and is reluctant to open her mouth. The posterior pharyngeal wall looks bulging on gentle inspection. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Retropharyngeal abscess; senior airway-aware assessment, IV antibiotics and contrast CT
Simple tonsillitis; oral antibiotics at home
Peritonsillar abscess; needle aspiration in the ward
Foreign body in the oesophagus; observe overnight

questions.correctOptionText: Retropharyngeal abscess; senior airway-aware assessment, IV antibiotics and contrast CT

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a deep neck space infection after pharyngitis in a young child.
distractorRationale.b: Does not explain torticollis and drooling.
distractorRationale.c: Unilateral tonsil bulge and uvular deviation are not described, and deep spread is likely.
distractorRationale.d: History is of infection, and this would delay treatment.

questions.explanation: Torticollis, drooling, refusal to swallow and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall after pharyngitis in a young child indicate a retropharyngeal abscess. The airway can close suddenly, so airway-aware senior review, IV antibiotics, contrast CT and drainage if a collection is present are required.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a painful decayed lower molar has a fever and tender, woody swelling beneath both sides of the jaw, with a raised tongue and drooling. His voice is muffled and he prefers to sit forward. What is the priority?

options.text: Secure and protect the airway with senior anaesthetic and ENT help, with IV antibiotics and CT
Outpatient oral antibiotics and dental review next week
Lie him flat for CT before any other action
Needle aspiration of the tongue base at the bedside

questions.correctOptionText: Secure and protect the airway with senior anaesthetic and ENT help, with IV antibiotics and CT

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Ludwig's angina threatens airway obstruction.

questions.explanation: Bilateral submandibular swelling with a raised tongue after a dental infection indicates Ludwig's angina, a deep neck space infection that can swiftly obstruct the airway. Airway management comes first, then IV antibiotics, contrast imaging and drainage.

questions.stem: An open surgical biopsy is the appropriate first investigation for a hard, painless neck node in a 60-year-old smoker suspected of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Ultrasound with fine needle aspiration or core biopsy and examination of the upper aerodigestive tract are first-line, because open biopsy risks seeding the tumour in the neck and complicates later surgery. Open biopsy is reserved for exceptional circumstances after specialist review.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman who smokes has had a hard, painless 3 cm lump in the upper left neck for five weeks and hoarseness for six weeks. Which is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Urgent suspected cancer referral to ENT for upper aerodigestive tract examination and imaging with sampling
Review in six months
Trial of antibiotics and discharge
Excision biopsy in primary care

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent suspected cancer referral to ENT for upper aerodigestive tract examination and imaging with sampling

distractorRationale.c: Persistent lump with red flags is not infective.

questions.explanation: A persistent hard unilateral neck lump with hoarseness in a smoker meets red-flag criteria for head and neck cancer, needing urgent referral under national suspected-cancer pathways (check current NICE guidance). Assessment includes nasendoscopy, ultrasound with FNA or core biopsy and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.stem: Describe the stepwise management of epistaxis, from first aid to surgical options, and explain which patients need admission.
markingGuide: First aid: lean forward, pinch soft nose 10 to 15 minutes, spit out blood
ABC assessment, IV access and bloods in heavy bleeds; check anticoagulants and blood pressure
Anterior bleeding point: cautery after topical anaesthetic
Anterior packing if cautery fails; posterior packing or balloon for posterior bleeding
Surgical or radiological: sphenopalatine ligation or embolisation
Admission: posterior packs, haemodynamic compromise, anticoagulation or bleeding disorder, significant comorbidity, failed packing
questions.explanation: Marks are given for a logical escalation ladder and for linking each step to its indication. Mentioning resuscitation and admission criteria shows safe practice.

questions.stem: Compare the presentation of acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess and deep neck space infection, and explain why airway management is a priority in the last two.
markingGuide: Tonsillitis: bilateral sore throat, fever, exudate, no trismus
Peritonsillar abscess: unilateral pain, trismus, muffled voice, displaced tonsil and uvula, drooling
Deep neck infection: neck swelling, torticollis, trismus, drooling, stridor, systemic toxicity
Airway risk from swelling of fascial spaces and floor of mouth (Ludwig's), and possible spread to mediastinum or carotid sheath
Management: senior airway management, IV antibiotics, CT with contrast, drainage
questions.explanation: A good answer contrasts local and bilateral disease, names the red-flag features of deep space spread and explains why swelling around the pharynx can suddenly close the airway.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker presents with a neck lump. Outline your history, examination and investigations, and list four red flags that would trigger an urgent referral.
markingGuide: History: duration, pain, fever, hoarseness, dysphagia, otalgia, weight loss, smoking and alcohol, past cancers
Examination: site by level, size, consistency, mobility, thyroid, salivary glands, skin and scalp, mouth, oropharynx, nasendoscopy
Investigations: ultrasound with FNA or core biopsy, CT or MRI, panendoscopy, thyroid function if relevant
Red flags (any four): lump over 3 weeks, persistent hoarseness, unilateral otalgia, persistent oral ulcer, dysphagia, weight loss, stridor, unilateral nasal obstruction
questions.explanation: The marker expects a systematic history and examination of the whole upper aerodigestive tract and appropriate non-excisional sampling. Four distinct red flags with a time criterion are needed.
